newsitem.title: UK: Britain says no return of Elgin marbles to Greece.
newsitem.headline: Britain says no return of Elgin marbles to Greece.

text.p: Britain's new Heritage Secretary on Sunday ruled out returning the Elgin marbles to Greece.
"We decided it was not a feasible or sensible option. We won't do it," Chris Smith said on BBC television.

Return of the classical sculptures, removed from the Acropolis in Athens and brought to London nearly 200 years ago,, has been a long-standing Greek demand, first put to the British government by the late culture minister Melina Mercouri.
Hopes had risen in Greece that, with Thursday's election of a new Labour government in Britain, the return of the treasures might now be closer at hand.
But Smith, whose ministry is responsible for cultural affairs, said the marbles were an integral part of the British Museum collection, visited by millions of people each year.
"It would make no sense at all to split up the British Museum collection in that way," he said. An entire room in the museum is dedicated to the marbles.
The sculptures came to Britain at the beginning of the 19th century, when Greece was still part of the Ottoman empire.

Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman court, shipped back almost all the bas-reliefs from the frieze of the ruined Parthenon in Athens, most of its pedimental structures, and a caryatid from the Erectheion.
He sold these to London's British Museum in 1816.
Smith said that returning the marbles could encourage other countries to demand the return of their treasures, unleashing a worldwide demand for the swapping of precious art works.
Those who oppose their return to Greece say the British Museum safeguarded them from damage while other sculptures at the Acropolis temples suffered from Athens' notorious air pollution.
